parts.title: Part 1
parts.transcript: Parroto IELTS Practice. Listening Test 7. You will hear a number of different recordings, and you will have to answer questions on what you hear. There will be time for you to read the instructions and questions, and you will have a chance to check your work. All the recordings will be played once only. The test is in four parts. Now turn to Part 1. Part 1. You will hear a woman asking a friend for advice about where to buy things for her new flat. First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 6. Now listen carefully and answer questions 1 to 6. Josh: Hi, Maya. How's the new flat? Maya: Hi, Josh. It's lovely, but it's still quite empty. I'm going to spend Saturday looking for furniture and things. You've lived here for ages, so I was hoping you could give me some ideas. Josh: Of course. Are you planning to go into town, or stay local? Maya: Local, if I can. I haven't got a car at the moment. Josh: Then the best area is Wharf Lane. Do you know it? It's the street that runs along beside the canal. Maya: Oh, where all the boats are moored? I've walked past it a few times. Josh: That's the one. There are lots of good shops there. What do you need most? Maya: A wardrobe, really. At the moment, all my clothes are still in boxes. Josh: Then you should try the furniture warehouse. It's huge, and everything's second-hand, so it's much cheaper than buying new. Maya: That sounds perfect. How do I find it? Josh: When you get to the end of Wharf Lane, you'll see the railway line. Go through the tunnel under the railway, and the warehouse is on your left. You can't miss it. Maya: Through the tunnel, then left. Got it. Is it open all day on Saturdays? Josh: No, it closes at one on Saturdays. And I'd get there by twelve thirty at the latest, because they stop taking payments about half an hour before closing. Maya: Twelve thirty. OK, that's useful to know. What about curtains and smaller things? I'd like the place to feel a bit more like home. Josh: Then go to the charity shop a bit further along. It's called Heron, like the bird. Maya: Heron? How do you spell that? Josh: H, E, R, O, N. It raises money for a wildlife charity, which is where the name comes from. The shop's quite small, but they've got some lovely things. Maya: How will I know which shop it is? Are there lots of them together? Josh: There are, but just look for the old bicycle outside. It's painted bright yellow, and it's got flowers in the basket. The owner puts it out every morning. Maya: That sounds sweet. And if I need paint and tools, is there anywhere nearby? Josh: There's a big DIY store on the ring road, but it's too far to walk. You can take the green bus, the number seventeen. It stops right outside. Maya: The green one. Great. Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 7 to 10. Now listen and answer questions 7 to 10. Josh: So what are you hoping to find in the warehouse, apart from a wardrobe? Maya: Well, I've already got a coat stand, but the hall is really dark. I thought I might get a mirror to hang there. It would make the space look bigger. Josh: Good idea. They always have lots of mirrors. And in the charity shop? Maya: Curtains are my priority. I don't need a rug, because all the floors are carpeted. But my sofa's quite old and plain, so I'd like a cushion to brighten it up a bit. Josh: Heron always has good cushions. They also have lots of glass and china. You could look for some vases for flowers. My sister found some beautiful ones there. Maya: Oh, I love having fresh flowers in the house. I've got more plates than I need, but vases would be great. Josh: And what do you need from the DIY store? Maya: I want to paint the bedroom. I've already got a roller, so I just need the paint and a new set of brushes. My old ones have gone really stiff. Josh: Make sure you get decent ones. Cheap brushes lose their hairs all over the wall. Maya: Good tip. Is there anywhere on Wharf Lane to get a coffee, by the way? Josh: Yes, there's a nice little cafe right by the canal. It gets very busy at the weekend, though. Maya: Thanks, Josh. That's been really helpful. Josh: No problem. Maybe I'll come and see the flat when it's finished. That is the end of Part 1. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to Part 1.

parts.title: Part 2
parts.transcript: Part 2. You will hear the organiser of a science festival for families talking on a local radio programme. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 16. Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 16. Presenter: The Brightwater Science Festival is coming back next month, and I'm delighted to welcome the organiser, Doctor Anna Reeve, to the studio. Anna, what can we look forward to this year? Anna: Thanks for having me. It's actually our tenth festival this year, so it's a special one for us. When we started, we had just a few talks in the town hall. Now we use the museum, the library and the university gardens as well, and last year more than eight thousand people came along. Presenter: That's quite a success story. So, what's on the programme this time? Anna: Thanks. Well, we've got a whole week of events for children and families, with scientists coming from universities all over the country. Let me tell you about a few of our workshops. Anna: First, there's Touch the Stars. This is a special astronomy session for children who are blind or partially sighted. Instead of looking through telescopes, children explore models of the planets and star maps with raised surfaces that they can feel with their fingers. Anna: Then there's Crime Lab. Children take on the roles of detectives and forensic scientists and act out the investigation of a mysterious crime, using real scientific techniques such as fingerprint analysis to solve it. Anna: Big Bang Club is a series of hands-on chemistry experiments. It's quite advanced, so it's only for eleven to thirteen year olds, I'm afraid. Younger children would find it too difficult. Anna: Creepy Crawlies is a chance to get close to spiders, beetles and other insects. We know that lots of children, and adults too, are frightened of spiders, and the session looks at where that fear comes from and helps children to feel more comfortable around them. Anna: Wave Makers is led by the engineer Sarah Okoye, who last year won a national award for her work on renewable energy. She'll show children how the power of the sea can be used to make electricity. The children won't be building anything themselves this time, but there'll be plenty of exciting demonstrations. Anna: And finally, Rainforest Rescue takes place in our giant greenhouse. It's designed to help children understand the rainforests of South America and the many threats they face, from logging to climate change. Most of the sessions are free, but places are limited, so please book online as soon as you can. Presenter: Is there anything for very young children? Anna: Yes. We have a storytelling tent where scientists read picture books about nature and space, and there's a quiet area with toys and puzzles for families who need a break. Parents often tell us that's one of the things they appreciate most. Before you hear the rest of the programme, you have some time to look at questions 17 to 20. Now listen and answer questions 17 to 20. Presenter: That all sounds fascinating. Anna, is there a book you'd recommend for young scientists? Anna: Yes. The Kitchen Scientist is my favourite at the moment. You won't have heard of the author, as it's her first book for children, and it's aimed at eight to twelve year olds, so it's not really for teenagers. It's full of experiments that use cheap, everyday things you'll already have at home, like vinegar, balloons and lemons, so there's no need to buy expensive kits. But what I like most is that every experiment comes with a really clear explanation of the science behind it. Some books just give you the instructions, and children never find out why things happen. The photos are only in black and white, which is a pity, but it really doesn't matter. Presenter: And where can people find it? Anna: It's in most bookshops, and the town library has several copies, so you don't even need to buy it. We'll also have a stall at the festival where the author will be signing copies on the Saturday afternoon. Presenter: And do you have any advice for parents who want to encourage their children's interest in science? Anna: Well, children ask a lot of questions, and parents often feel they have to know all the answers. But it's fine to admit that you don't know. In fact, it's a great opportunity to find out together. Some parents buy expensive equipment like microscopes, but you really don't need to. And many museums and science centres run free events at weekends and during the school holidays, so do look out for those. Anna: Some parents ask their children to keep a science diary, but I'd be careful with that, as children can see it as extra homework. And there's no need to ban screens completely. There are some excellent science programmes for children, and they can be a great starting point. Presenter: Anna, thank you very much. That's really useful advice. That is the end of Part 2. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to Part 2.

parts.title: Part 3
parts.transcript: Part 3. You will hear two trainee science teachers, Ella and Tom, discussing an experiment for one of Ella's classes. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 25. Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 25. Tom: Hi, Ella. How's your teaching placement going? Mine's going really well, actually. The staff at my school have been very supportive, and I've got a lovely Year 8 class. Ella: Oh, it's OK, but I'm finding my Year 10 class quite difficult. Tom: Are they badly behaved? Ella: No, not at all. They're polite, they do what I ask, and their test results are actually fine. It's just that they never ask any questions. They don't seem curious about anything, and I find that really disappointing. Tom: That's a shame. Science should make people curious. Ella: Exactly. And I have to design an experiment for them as part of my placement. I was thinking about something on water quality, getting them to collect samples from different rivers and streams around the town and then test them in the lab. Tom: It sounds interesting, and the results could be really good. But think about the organisation. You'd have to take them out on trips to collect the samples, which means risk assessments, permission letters for parents, extra staff. It could take weeks to arrange. Ella: Hmm, you're right. Maybe it should be something they can do in the lab. Tom: I think that would be sensible, at least for your first experiment. You can always plan a trip later in the year, once you know the class better. Ella: True. And my supervisor did say to keep things simple to begin with. Tom: What about growing plants? Ella: Wouldn't that take too long? Tom: Not if you use cress. It germinates in a couple of days. Ella: But if we found something out about cress, it wouldn't necessarily tell us anything about real crops grown on farms, would it? Tom: No, that's true. The results wouldn't necessarily apply to farm crops. But any school experiment has limitations like that. It's unavoidable. Ella: I suppose so. So what could we investigate? Tom: Well, you could look at how different fertilisers affect growth. Ella: Maybe. Or what about salt? I read that in some coastal areas, rising sea levels are making the soil salty. We could find out whether seeds can still germinate when they're given salty water. Tom: I like that. It's a simple question, can the seeds germinate or not, and it links to a real-world problem, which might get them interested. Ella: That's what I was hoping. Tom: How long would you give them? Ella: Probably two lessons, a week apart. One to set everything up, and one to measure the results and discuss them. I'd like them to write up the experiment for homework, too. Tom: That seems about right. And it'll be good practice for their exams, because they always have to describe a method and explain their results. Tom: And if it goes well, you could do a follow-up experiment. You could keep the salt the same and change the temperature. Ella: Or I could compare different amounts of light. Actually, I think light would be better, because temperature is hard to control in the school lab. I'll probably try light next. Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 26 to 30. Now listen and answer questions 26 to 30. Ella: So, can we talk through the procedure? Tom: Sure. I did something similar at college, actually. Ella: Great. First, the seeds. Do they all need to be the same size? Tom: Size doesn't really matter with cress. What's important is that they're all the same variety, so buy them all from one packet. Ella: OK. Then I'll put them on damp cotton wool in small dishes. I'll have two groups, with ten dishes in each. But how will the students tell the groups apart? Tom: Just stick labels on the dishes. They can write A or B on each one, and the date. Ella: Right. Group A gets ordinary tap water. Group B gets exactly the same amount of water, but with salt added. I did think about using sugar instead, but salt is more realistic. Tom: Yes, salt's definitely better. Ella: How much salt should I use, though? Tom: I'd start with about a teaspoon in a litre of water. If none of the seeds germinate at all, you won't learn very much, so you don't want it to be too salty. Ella: That makes sense. Ella: And both groups will be on the same windowsill, so they get the same amount of sunlight. Tom: Good. You should also cover each dish with cling film. Otherwise there'll be a lot of evaporation, and the cotton wool will dry out, especially by a sunny window. Ella: I wouldn't have thought of that. And then, after a week, the students measure the seedlings? Tom: Yes. They can use a ruler to measure the height of each seedling in millimetres, and count how many seeds have germinated in each dish. Then they can work out the averages for each group. Ella: That sounds manageable. I think they might even enjoy it. Tom: And you could ask them to predict what will happen before they start. That usually gets them more involved, because they want to find out if they were right. Ella: That's a great idea. Maybe they'll even start asking questions! Tom: I'm sure they will. Let me know how it goes. That is the end of Part 3. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to Part 3.

parts.title: Part 4
parts.transcript: Part 4. You will hear part of an environmental science lecture about light pollution. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40. Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40. Lecturer: Today I'm going to talk about a form of pollution that has received much less attention than air or water pollution, and that's light pollution. By this, I mean artificial light that shines where it isn't needed or wanted, especially at night. It's a relatively recent problem. For most of human history, nights were dark, and it's only in the last hundred years or so, with the spread of electric lighting, that this has changed. Today, around eighty per cent of the world's population lives under skies that are affected by artificial light. Lecturer: The sources of light pollution are all around us. The most obvious is street lighting, but many other sources contribute. In city centres, illuminated billboards advertising everything from phones to fast food often stay switched on all night. Sports stadiums are another major source, as their floodlights can be seen from many kilometres away. And in some agricultural regions, a surprising amount of light comes from greenhouses, where crops such as tomatoes are grown under powerful lamps through the winter months. In some places, the glow from these greenhouses can be seen from aircraft flying high overhead. Lecturer: Light pollution has serious effects on wildlife. Many birds migrate at night, using the stars to help them navigate. Brightly lit buildings can confuse them, and every year large numbers of migrating birds are killed when they fly into illuminated towers and office blocks. Lecturer: On beaches, newly hatched sea turtles normally find their way to the water by moving towards the brightest horizon, which is usually the moonlit sea. But where there are hotels and streetlights along the shore, the young turtles often head inland instead, and many of them die. Insects are also badly affected. Moths in particular are attracted to artificial lights, and many circle them until they die of exhaustion or are eaten by predators. In some countries, hotels near nesting beaches are now required to turn off or cover their outside lights during the nesting season, and volunteers patrol the beaches at night to help any young turtles that go the wrong way. Lecturer: It's not only wildlife that suffers. Light pollution also affects our view of the night sky. It has been estimated that more than a third of the world's population can no longer see the Milky Way, and in large cities, most people can see only a handful of the brightest stars. For astronomers, this is a real problem, and many observatories have had to be built on remote mountains, far from any towns. Lecturer: I'd now like to tell you about an interesting study carried out by researchers in Switzerland, who wanted to find out how street lighting affects plants. They installed streetlights in several meadows in the countryside where there had been no artificial light before, and compared them with similar meadows that remained dark. They found that in the lit meadows, night-time visits to flowers by insects fell by more than sixty per cent. As a result, one of the plants they studied produced significantly fewer fruits than the same plant in the dark meadows. What's more, the insects that visit flowers during the day did not make up for this loss. Lecturer: So what can be done? The good news is that, unlike many other kinds of pollution, light pollution can be reduced quickly and cheaply. First of all, lights with a warmer colour, such as amber, attract far fewer insects than bright white or blue ones. Secondly, lights can be fitted with shields, so that the light shines down onto the ground where it's needed, rather than up into the sky. And finally, many lights don't need to be on all night. Motion sensors can switch lights on only when someone is actually there. Some towns have also started switching off street lights in quiet areas after midnight, and there has been no increase in crime as a result. Of course, none of these measures means living in darkness. The aim is simply to use light more carefully, so that we get the benefits of lighting without the costs to wildlife and to our view of the night sky. That is the end of Part 4. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to Part 4. That is the end of the listening test.

parts.title: Part 2
parts.transcript: Part 2. You will hear the organiser of a science festival for families talking on a local radio programme. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 16. Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 16. Presenter: The Brightwater Science Festival is coming back next month, and I'm delighted to welcome the organiser, Doctor Anna Reeve, to the studio. Anna, what can we look forward to this year? Anna: Thanks for having me. It's actually our tenth festival this year, so it's a special one for us. When we started, we had just a few talks in the town hall. Now we use the museum, the library and the university gardens as well, and last year more than eight thousand people came along. Presenter: That's quite a success story. So, what's on the programme this time? Anna: Thanks. Well, we've got a whole week of events for children and families, with scientists coming from universities all over the country. Let me tell you about a few of our workshops. Anna: First, there's Touch the Stars. This is a special astronomy session for children who are blind or partially sighted. Instead of looking through telescopes, children explore models of the planets and star maps with raised surfaces that they can feel with their fingers. Anna: Then there's Crime Lab. Children take on the roles of detectives and forensic scientists and act out the investigation of a mysterious crime, using real scientific techniques such as fingerprint analysis to solve it. Anna: Big Bang Club is a series of hands-on chemistry experiments. It's quite advanced, so it's only for eleven to thirteen year olds, I'm afraid. Younger children would find it too difficult. Anna: Creepy Crawlies is a chance to get close to spiders, beetles and other insects. We know that lots of children, and adults too, are frightened of spiders, and the session looks at where that fear comes from and helps children to feel more comfortable around them. Anna: Wave Makers is led by the engineer Sarah Okoye, who last year won a national award for her work on renewable energy. She'll show children how the power of the sea can be used to make electricity. The children won't be building anything themselves this time, but there'll be plenty of exciting demonstrations. Anna: And finally, Rainforest Rescue takes place in our giant greenhouse. It's designed to help children understand the rainforests of South America and the many threats they face, from logging to climate change. Most of the sessions are free, but places are limited, so please book online as soon as you can. Presenter: Is there anything for very young children? Anna: Yes. We have a storytelling tent where scientists read picture books about nature and space, and there's a quiet area with toys and puzzles for families who need a break. Parents often tell us that's one of the things they appreciate most. Before you hear the rest of the programme, you have some time to look at questions 17 to 20. Now listen and answer questions 17 to 20. Presenter: That all sounds fascinating. Anna, is there a book you'd recommend for young scientists? Anna: Yes. The Kitchen Scientist is my favourite at the moment. You won't have heard of the author, as it's her first book for children, and it's aimed at eight to twelve year olds, so it's not really for teenagers. It's full of experiments that use cheap, everyday things you'll already have at home, like vinegar, balloons and lemons, so there's no need to buy expensive kits. But what I like most is that every experiment comes with a really clear explanation of the science behind it. Some books just give you the instructions, and children never find out why things happen. The photos are only in black and white, which is a pity, but it really doesn't matter. Presenter: And where can people find it? Anna: It's in most bookshops, and the town library has several copies, so you don't even need to buy it. We'll also have a stall at the festival where the author will be signing copies on the Saturday afternoon. Presenter: And do you have any advice for parents who want to encourage their children's interest in science? Anna: Well, children ask a lot of questions, and parents often feel they have to know all the answers. But it's fine to admit that you don't know. In fact, it's a great opportunity to find out together. Some parents buy expensive equipment like microscopes, but you really don't need to. And many museums and science centres run free events at weekends and during the school holidays, so do look out for those. Anna: Some parents ask their children to keep a science diary, but I'd be careful with that, as children can see it as extra homework. And there's no need to ban screens completely. There are some excellent science programmes for children, and they can be a great starting point. Presenter: Anna, thank you very much. That's really useful advice. That is the end of Part 2. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to Part 2.

parts.title: Part 3
parts.transcript: Part 3. You will hear two trainee science teachers, Ella and Tom, discussing an experiment for one of Ella's classes. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 25. Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 25. Tom: Hi, Ella. How's your teaching placement going? Mine's going really well, actually. The staff at my school have been very supportive, and I've got a lovely Year 8 class. Ella: Oh, it's OK, but I'm finding my Year 10 class quite difficult. Tom: Are they badly behaved? Ella: No, not at all. They're polite, they do what I ask, and their test results are actually fine. It's just that they never ask any questions. They don't seem curious about anything, and I find that really disappointing. Tom: That's a shame. Science should make people curious. Ella: Exactly. And I have to design an experiment for them as part of my placement. I was thinking about something on water quality, getting them to collect samples from different rivers and streams around the town and then test them in the lab. Tom: It sounds interesting, and the results could be really good. But think about the organisation. You'd have to take them out on trips to collect the samples, which means risk assessments, permission letters for parents, extra staff. It could take weeks to arrange. Ella: Hmm, you're right. Maybe it should be something they can do in the lab. Tom: I think that would be sensible, at least for your first experiment. You can always plan a trip later in the year, once you know the class better. Ella: True. And my supervisor did say to keep things simple to begin with. Tom: What about growing plants? Ella: Wouldn't that take too long? Tom: Not if you use cress. It germinates in a couple of days. Ella: But if we found something out about cress, it wouldn't necessarily tell us anything about real crops grown on farms, would it? Tom: No, that's true. The results wouldn't necessarily apply to farm crops. But any school experiment has limitations like that. It's unavoidable. Ella: I suppose so. So what could we investigate? Tom: Well, you could look at how different fertilisers affect growth. Ella: Maybe. Or what about salt? I read that in some coastal areas, rising sea levels are making the soil salty. We could find out whether seeds can still germinate when they're given salty water. Tom: I like that. It's a simple question, can the seeds germinate or not, and it links to a real-world problem, which might get them interested. Ella: That's what I was hoping. Tom: How long would you give them? Ella: Probably two lessons, a week apart. One to set everything up, and one to measure the results and discuss them. I'd like them to write up the experiment for homework, too. Tom: That seems about right. And it'll be good practice for their exams, because they always have to describe a method and explain their results. Tom: And if it goes well, you could do a follow-up experiment. You could keep the salt the same and change the temperature. Ella: Or I could compare different amounts of light. Actually, I think light would be better, because temperature is hard to control in the school lab. I'll probably try light next. Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 26 to 30. Now listen and answer questions 26 to 30. Ella: So, can we talk through the procedure? Tom: Sure. I did something similar at college, actually. Ella: Great. First, the seeds. Do they all need to be the same size? Tom: Size doesn't really matter with cress. What's important is that they're all the same variety, so buy them all from one packet. Ella: OK. Then I'll put them on damp cotton wool in small dishes. I'll have two groups, with ten dishes in each. But how will the students tell the groups apart? Tom: Just stick labels on the dishes. They can write A or B on each one, and the date. Ella: Right. Group A gets ordinary tap water. Group B gets exactly the same amount of water, but with salt added. I did think about using sugar instead, but salt is more realistic. Tom: Yes, salt's definitely better. Ella: How much salt should I use, though? Tom: I'd start with about a teaspoon in a litre of water. If none of the seeds germinate at all, you won't learn very much, so you don't want it to be too salty. Ella: That makes sense. Ella: And both groups will be on the same windowsill, so they get the same amount of sunlight. Tom: Good. You should also cover each dish with cling film. Otherwise there'll be a lot of evaporation, and the cotton wool will dry out, especially by a sunny window. Ella: I wouldn't have thought of that. And then, after a week, the students measure the seedlings? Tom: Yes. They can use a ruler to measure the height of each seedling in millimetres, and count how many seeds have germinated in each dish. Then they can work out the averages for each group. Ella: That sounds manageable. I think they might even enjoy it. Tom: And you could ask them to predict what will happen before they start. That usually gets them more involved, because they want to find out if they were right. Ella: That's a great idea. Maybe they'll even start asking questions! Tom: I'm sure they will. Let me know how it goes. That is the end of Part 3. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to Part 3.

parts.title: Part 4
parts.transcript: Part 4. You will hear part of an environmental science lecture about light pollution. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40. Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40. Lecturer: Today I'm going to talk about a form of pollution that has received much less attention than air or water pollution, and that's light pollution. By this, I mean artificial light that shines where it isn't needed or wanted, especially at night. It's a relatively recent problem. For most of human history, nights were dark, and it's only in the last hundred years or so, with the spread of electric lighting, that this has changed. Today, around eighty per cent of the world's population lives under skies that are affected by artificial light. Lecturer: The sources of light pollution are all around us. The most obvious is street lighting, but many other sources contribute. In city centres, illuminated billboards advertising everything from phones to fast food often stay switched on all night. Sports stadiums are another major source, as their floodlights can be seen from many kilometres away. And in some agricultural regions, a surprising amount of light comes from greenhouses, where crops such as tomatoes are grown under powerful lamps through the winter months. In some places, the glow from these greenhouses can be seen from aircraft flying high overhead. Lecturer: Light pollution has serious effects on wildlife. Many birds migrate at night, using the stars to help them navigate. Brightly lit buildings can confuse them, and every year large numbers of migrating birds are killed when they fly into illuminated towers and office blocks. Lecturer: On beaches, newly hatched sea turtles normally find their way to the water by moving towards the brightest horizon, which is usually the moonlit sea. But where there are hotels and streetlights along the shore, the young turtles often head inland instead, and many of them die. Insects are also badly affected. Moths in particular are attracted to artificial lights, and many circle them until they die of exhaustion or are eaten by predators. In some countries, hotels near nesting beaches are now required to turn off or cover their outside lights during the nesting season, and volunteers patrol the beaches at night to help any young turtles that go the wrong way. Lecturer: It's not only wildlife that suffers. Light pollution also affects our view of the night sky. It has been estimated that more than a third of the world's population can no longer see the Milky Way, and in large cities, most people can see only a handful of the brightest stars. For astronomers, this is a real problem, and many observatories have had to be built on remote mountains, far from any towns. Lecturer: I'd now like to tell you about an interesting study carried out by researchers in Switzerland, who wanted to find out how street lighting affects plants. They installed streetlights in several meadows in the countryside where there had been no artificial light before, and compared them with similar meadows that remained dark. They found that in the lit meadows, night-time visits to flowers by insects fell by more than sixty per cent. As a result, one of the plants they studied produced significantly fewer fruits than the same plant in the dark meadows. What's more, the insects that visit flowers during the day did not make up for this loss. Lecturer: So what can be done? The good news is that, unlike many other kinds of pollution, light pollution can be reduced quickly and cheaply. First of all, lights with a warmer colour, such as amber, attract far fewer insects than bright white or blue ones. Secondly, lights can be fitted with shields, so that the light shines down onto the ground where it's needed, rather than up into the sky. And finally, many lights don't need to be on all night. Motion sensors can switch lights on only when someone is actually there. Some towns have also started switching off street lights in quiet areas after midnight, and there has been no increase in crime as a result. Of course, none of these measures means living in darkness. The aim is simply to use light more carefully, so that we get the benefits of lighting without the costs to wildlife and to our view of the night sky. That is the end of Part 4. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to Part 4. That is the end of the listening test.
